segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About that time King Herod laid hands on some who belonged to the assembly, to do them harm.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He had James the brother of John killed with the sword.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw that this pleased the Jews, he went on to arrest Peter as well. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having seized him, he put him in prison, handing him over to four squads of four soldiers each to guard him, intending to bring him out before the people after the Passover.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Peter was kept in the prison, but prayer for him was being earnestly made to God by the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Herod was about to bring him out, that very night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while guards in front of the door kept watch over the prison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And suddenly an angel of the Lord stood there, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Get up quickly!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the chains fell from his hands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The angel said to him,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Fasten your belt and put on your sandals.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he did so. Then he said to him,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went out and followed, and he did not know that what was happening through the angel was real; he thought he was seeing a vision.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After passing the first guard post and the second, they came to the iron gate leading into the city, which opened for them by itself. They went out and walked the length of one street, and immediately the angel left him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Peter came to himself, he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel and rescued me from Herod’s hand and from everything the people of the Jews were expecting.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was also called Mark, where a good number had gathered and were praying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he knocked at the door of the gateway, a slave girl named Rhoda came to answer,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gateway but ran in and reported that Peter was standing in front of the gateway.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to her,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are out of your mind!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But she kept insisting that it was so. And they kept saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is his angel.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened they saw him and were astounded.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Report these things to James and the brothers and sisters.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he left and went to another place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When day came, there was no small commotion among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Herod searched for him and did not find him; he interrogated the guards and ordered them led away to execution. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now he was furious with the people of Tyre and Sidon. But with one mind they came to him, and having won over Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country was fed from the king’s.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On an appointed day Herod, dressed in royal robes and seated on the platform, was delivering a public address to them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the populace kept shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The voice of a god, not of a human being!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give the glory to God, and he was eaten by worms and died.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the word of God kept growing and multiplying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Barnabas and Saul returned, having completed their service in Jerusalem, taking along with them John, who was called Mark.

notes.note: This is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great and nephew of the Herod Antipas who appears in the Gospels. He ruled Judea as king under Roman patronage from AD 41 until his death in AD 44, which helps date the events of this chapter.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” everywhere the word occurs, so that the reader sees one Greek word.

notes.phrase: four squads of four soldiers each
notes.note: Sixteen soldiers in all, probably one squad of four for each of the four watches of the night. Verse 6 fits this, with two soldiers chained to Peter and two on guard at the door.

Luke uses “Passover” for the whole week-long festival, including the days of Unleavened Bread mentioned in verse 3. Herod intended to wait until the festival was over before staging a public trial. The King James Version’s “Easter” here is an anachronism.

In this period the word normally meant a female slave, not a hired servant. Most English versions soften it to “servant girl” or “maid.” A household large enough to host a gathering and to have a gateway would ordinarily have owned slaves.

Many Jews of the period believed that a person had a guardian angel, and some later sources suggest such an angel could resemble the person. The speakers assume that what stands at the gate is this heavenly counterpart, not Peter himself. Some interpreters think they mean that Peter has been killed and that this is his spirit, but the word does not normally mean “ghost.”

This is not James the brother of John, who was killed in verse 2. It is James the brother of Jesus, who appears from this point on as the leading figure in the Jerusalem assembly (Acts 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19).

The Greek masculine plural was the normal way to address or refer to a mixed group of fellow members, and the gathering in this house included women. “Brothers” is the traditional rendering; many recent versions use “brothers and sisters” or “believers.”

The Greek says only that Herod ordered the guards “to be led away.” The verb was a common idiom for taking someone off to execution, and under Roman practice a guard who lost a prisoner could suffer the prisoner’s penalty, so most translators understand it that way. It could mean only that they were led off to prison.

The Greek has no article, and the crowd in Caesarea is largely pagan, so “a god” is the natural sense. Honoring rulers as divine was common in the eastern Roman world. “The voice of God” is grammatically possible but less likely on these speakers’ lips.

The same verb describes the angel striking Peter to wake him in verse 7; the repetition is probably deliberate, one blow rescuing and the other judging. The Jewish historian Josephus independently records that Agrippa, hailed as more than mortal in Caesarea, did not reject the flattery, was seized by violent abdominal pain and died some days later. Luke’s account is compressed and need not mean that he died on the spot.

The best-attested reading is “to Jerusalem,” which is difficult because Barnabas and Saul were already there (11:30) and next appear in Antioch (13:1). Other manuscripts read “from Jerusalem,” probably a scribal correction, and most English versions follow them. The edition translated here keeps “to Jerusalem” but punctuates so that the phrase goes with the service, which this translation renders “their service in Jerusalem”; the return is then to Antioch.

The word was an everyday term for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf; here it is the delivery of famine relief from Antioch (11:29–30). Older versions have “ministry” and many modern ones “mission.” “Service” avoids the clerical overtone of “ministry” and keeps the link with the related words for “serve” and “servant.”

candidates.reason: The same word names Pilate’s and Gallio’s judicial seat and the judgment seat of God and of Christ (Rom 14:10; 2 Cor 5:10), and versions vary between throne, tribunal, platform and judgment seat.
The plural for community members recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translators differ between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “believers.”
It recurs in the Gospels, Acts and Galatians 4, and the choice between “slave” and “servant” or “maid” should match the decision for the other slave vocabulary.
A favorite word in Acts, variously rendered “with one accord,” “together” or “unanimously,” whose repetition the reader should be able to see.
It occurs in Acts 12, 17 and 19 for a civic body or gathered citizenry and needs to be kept distinct from the renderings of λαός, ὄχλος and ἐκκλησία.
